headline: A 2014 Senate bill that would have expanded hunting, fishing, and shooting access on federal lands and changed several related wildlife rules, but it did not pass.
what_it_does: If adopted, this bill would have changed several existing programs to make it easier to hunt, fish, and shoot on public land. It would have made federal Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service lands open to these activities unless the managing agency closed them. It also would have exempted firearm and ammunition parts, and fishing gear such as lead sinkers, from certain chemical rules under the Toxic Substances Control Act. It would have reauthorized several land and wetland conservation programs and made other changes to wildlife rules.

who_it_affects.how: They would have gained wider access to BLM and Forest Service lands for hunting and fishing unless those lands were closed.
They would have had more access to federal public land for shooting and more state funding could have gone to public target ranges.

who_it_affects.group: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers and sport fishing gear makers
who_it_affects.how: Their components would have been exempt from certain chemical regulations under the Toxic Substances Control Act.
They could have used more Pittman-Robertson funds for public target ranges and issued temporary electronic duck stamps with federal approval.
Rules for what counts as a baited area for hunting migratory game birds would have been revised.

who_it_affects.group: Hunters who bring polar bear trophies into the US
who_it_affects.how: The Secretary of the Interior would have been required to issue import permits for polar bear parts from sport hunts in Canada taken before May 15, 2008.
